questions.question: Why is bidirectional context valuable for many language understanding tasks?
options: It lets the model use clues from both the left and right of a token
It guarantees linear-time generation
It removes the need for tokenization
It forces all tasks to use the same output head
questions.explanation: Tasks like classification, NER, and retrieval benefit from seeing the full surrounding context of each token. A bidirectional encoder can use evidence from both directions instead of being restricted to only past tokens.

questions.question: Why was pretraining one large language model and then fine-tuning it such a big shift for NLP?
options: It eliminated the need for labeled data entirely
It let each task reuse broad language knowledge instead of training a fresh model from scratch
It made recurrent models deeper
It replaced embeddings with hand-written features
questions.explanation: Before BERT, many NLP tasks trained separate models on small labeled datasets. Pretraining created a shared language backbone that could be adapted with a small task-specific head, greatly improving parameter efficiency.

questions.question: What masking recipe does BERT use for the tokens selected for prediction?
options: 100% replaced with [MASK]
50% [MASK], 50% unchanged
80% [MASK], 10% random token, 10% unchanged
10% [MASK], 80% random token, 10% unchanged
questions.explanation: The lesson states that BERT selects 15% of tokens, then applies an 80/10/10 split to those selected positions. Most become [MASK], some become random tokens, and some stay unchanged while still being predicted.

questions.question: Why doesn't BERT replace every selected token with [MASK]?
options: Because [MASK] is too expensive to store in the vocabulary
Because [MASK] never appears at inference time, so always using it would create a train-test mismatch
Because the encoder cannot process masked tokens
Because RoPE requires some original tokens to stay visible
questions.explanation: The docs explain that [MASK] is a pretraining artifact and does not appear in normal downstream inference. Mixing in random and unchanged tokens reduces that distribution shift so the encoder learns to handle more realistic inputs.

questions.question: According to the lesson, when is an encoder like BERT still the right tool in 2026?
options: For autoregressive text generation and chat
For retrieval, classification, and structured extraction where bidirectional embeddings matter
Only for image generation
Only when you need next-sentence prediction
questions.explanation: The lesson says encoder-only models remain strong for classification, retrieval, reranking, and token labeling. They are faster per token than decoders for these tasks and their bidirectional representations make better embeddings.
